content:
A temple, math or religious and charitable trust website in India needs to do four jobs well: give devotees accurate darshan and puja timings and festival schedules; let them book sevas, pujas and annadan sponsorships online with a clear confirmation; accept donations into the right fund with a correct receipt (and an 80G certificate only if the trust actually holds that approval); and publish enough about the trust (registration, trustees, use of funds) that a devotee who has never visited believes the money reaches the temple. Most trust websites we see do the first job on a static page that was last updated years ago, and handle the rest through phone calls and a UPI QR image. This guide covers how to build the whole thing properly, as part of NGO website development in India for religious and charitable trusts.

It is written for trustees, temple managers and administrative staff of temples, maths, gurudwara and church committees, dargah committees and other religious and charitable public trusts, especially in Maharashtra, where most such trusts are registered under the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950 with the office of the Charity Commissioner. Much of it applies equally elsewhere in India. Tax and FCRA points here are general; your chartered accountant and legal adviser should confirm what applies to your trust.

## Who visits a temple or trust website, and what they want

Before choosing features, be clear about who the site serves:

- **Local devotees** checking today's timings, festival dates, or whether the temple is open during an eclipse or a special event.
- **Out-of-town visitors and pilgrims** planning a trip: how to reach, where to stay nearby, dress code, what can be carried inside, parking.
- **Devotees who want to book a seva or puja,** sometimes in their own name, sometimes for a family member, sometimes from abroad.
- **Donors,** for general donations, specific funds (annadan, gaushala, building renovation, education) or in memory of someone.
- **Families and diaspora devotees** who cannot visit and want to watch aarti or a festival live.
- **Researchers, journalists and government offices** looking for the trust's history, registration and contacts.

A good site serves each group in two taps or fewer from the home page. The structure below follows from that.

## The pages a trust website needs

### Timings and calendar

The most visited page on almost every temple site. Build it as structured data the office can edit, not as a typed paragraph:

- daily darshan, aarti and puja timings, with separate rows for weekdays, weekends and special days;
- closures and changed timings (eclipses, festivals, renovation) entered as dated exceptions, so the page shows the right timings for today automatically;
- a festival calendar for the year, with dates according to the panchang the trust follows;
- a "last updated" note, so visitors know the information is current.

Because devotees often search "[temple name] timings", consistency with your Google Business Profile matters: the same hours, the same special-hours exceptions. When timings change, update both on the same day.

### Visiting information

How to reach by road, rail and air, parking, accessibility (ramps, wheelchair availability, a separate queue for elderly or disabled devotees if the temple has one), dress code, items not permitted, cloakroom and footwear stand, and nearby accommodation the trust runs or recommends. Clear, practical, and in the languages your devotees use.

### Seva and puja booking

This is where a website saves the office the most time. A booking system for a temple should:

- list each seva or puja with a description, the date options (daily, specific days, festival-only), the time, and the contribution;
- collect the details the priest needs: name of the devotee, gotra and nakshatra where relevant, names of family members, and the intention (sankalpa) if the seva requires it;
- allow booking on behalf of someone else, with separate fields for the person booking and the person in whose name the seva is performed;
- respect daily capacity limits, so the office does not receive more bookings than the priests can perform;
- send a confirmation by email and, if the trust uses it, by WhatsApp, with the booking reference, date, time and what to bring;
- produce a daily schedule for the office and priests (printable), listing every booking with the names to be recited;
- handle cancellations and date changes according to a written policy.

Build it so the temple office can change prices, capacity and dates without a developer. The most common failure in temple booking systems is that a festival date changes and nobody can update the site.

A note on terminology. Whether a seva payment is treated as a donation or a payment for a service has tax and receipt consequences. Agree with your CA how each seva category should be recorded and receipted, and set the website up to follow that, rather than labelling everything "donation".

### Donations

Donation pages for a trust have the same fundamentals as any NGO donation page (see our guide to [designing a donation page donors actually complete](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026/)), plus a few points specific to religious trusts:

- **Funds, not just amounts.** Devotees often want their gift to go to something specific: annadan (meals), gaushala, a festival, building renovation, education or medical aid run by the trust. Let them choose, and make sure each fund is set up as a separate head in your accounts so the money is tracked against it.
- **Sponsorship with real costs.** "Sponsor annadan for one day" works when the amount is based on the trust's actual cost. Publish what a day's annadan costs only if the figure comes from your accounts, and update it when costs change.
- **In-memory and occasion giving.** Birthdays, anniversaries and remembrance days are common reasons to give. Collect the occasion and the name, and if the trust performs a puja or annadan on that date, say so clearly and confirm it.
- **Receipts that match your registration.** Every receipt should carry the trust's registered name, registration number, address and PAN, the donor's name, the amount, the date, the mode of payment, the fund, and a unique receipt number generated by the system.

### 80G: only if the trust has it

This is the point where trust websites most often go wrong. Section 80G deductions are available only for donations to institutions that hold a valid 80G approval, and many trusts whose objects are wholly religious do not qualify for one under the rules as they stand. Some trusts run separate charitable activities (a school, a hospital, relief work) and hold approvals for those. Others hold no 80G approval at all.

So:

- **Do not display "Donations are tax-exempt under 80G"** unless the trust holds a current approval, and only for the funds and activities it covers.
- **If you hold 80G,** show the approval number and validity on the donation page, collect the donor's PAN for donations where the certificate will be issued, and make sure the receipts and annual donor statements follow the format and filing process your CA uses. The Income Tax Act, 2025 has renumbered sections and forms; your CA will know what the current names are.
- **If only some funds qualify,** make it impossible for a donor to believe a non-eligible gift will get a certificate. Show the 80G note only next to eligible funds.

Getting this wrong annoys donors at tax time and can create trouble for the trust.

### Donations from abroad: FCRA

Devotees living abroad often want to donate. Any trust receiving foreign contribution must hold registration or prior permission under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and the Act specifically covers organisations with a definite religious programme. Foreign contribution must also be received into the trust's designated FCRA account at the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch, and kept separate from domestic funds.

For the website, that means:

- **If the trust has no FCRA registration,** the donation form must not accept foreign contributions. Ask donors to confirm they are Indian citizens donating from Indian sources, and do not offer international card payments for donations. Explain politely why.
- **If the trust is registered,** create a separate donation path for foreign contribution that routes to the FCRA account, collects the information your CA needs, and issues receipts accordingly.
- **Be careful with NRIs.** Whether a gift from a person of Indian origin abroad counts as foreign contribution depends on the person's citizenship and source of funds; let your legal adviser write the wording on the form.

### Live darshan and festival streams

For many families and diaspora devotees, live aarti is the most valued feature. Practical choices:

- **Stream to YouTube and embed** on the website, rather than hosting video yourself. It costs nothing in bandwidth and handles large audiences.
- **Use a lightweight embed** that loads the player only when tapped, so the timings page stays fast. Our general advice on [multilingual sites](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-multilingual-hindi-marathi-donation-site-2026/) and fast pages applies here too.
- **Publish a streaming schedule** and keep recordings of major festivals in a playlist.
- **Respect sanctum rules.** Some temples do not permit filming of the sanctum. Decide what is filmed and say so.

### About the trust, and transparency

Devotees giving online want to know who runs the trust. A clear "About the trust" section should include:

- the trust's history (accurate, with sources where traditions are cited);
- registration details: name as registered, registration number, the Charity Commissioner's office (for Maharashtra trusts), PAN;
- current trustees and key office-bearers;
- the activities the trust runs beyond worship (annadan, education, medical aid, relief);
- annual reports or a summary of income and how funds were used, as the trust decides to publish;
- contacts for the office, with the hours when it answers phones.

Our guide to [building a transparency and impact section](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-transparency-impact-reporting-2026/) explains how to present financial summaries in a way donors understand.

## Languages and accessibility

Many temple websites serve devotees who are more comfortable in Marathi, Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati or another language than in English. Pick the two or three languages your devotees use most and translate the high-traffic pages properly: timings, visiting information, booking and donation. Avoid machine-translated text for religious terms; have someone from the trust check every page.

Many devotees are older. Use large, readable type, good contrast, buttons that are easy to tap, and simple forms. Make sure the booking and donation forms work with a screen reader and without a mouse.

## WhatsApp: useful, but keep it clean

WhatsApp is how many devotees prefer to receive booking confirmations, festival reminders and receipts. With the [WhatsApp Business API](/whatsapp/business-api), a trust can send automated booking confirmations and receipts and, with devotees' opt-in, festival announcements. Two cautions: send only to people who opted in, with a simple way to stop; and do not let festival broadcasts become daily messages, or devotees will block the number that also carries their receipts.

## Security and fraud: protect devotees and the trust's name

Popular temples are targets for fake websites, fake social media pages and fake UPI QR codes claiming to collect donations or sell "VIP darshan" passes. The trust website should:

- state clearly which domain, which bank accounts and which UPI IDs are official, and that the trust never sells darshan passes through third parties (if that is true);
- publish a notice on how to report fakes;
- use HTTPS, keep the CMS and plugins updated, use strong passwords and two-factor authentication for admin accounts, and keep tested backups;
- restrict admin access to named people, removing access when someone leaves the office.

A trust's donation and booking pages handle money and personal data, and should be treated with the same care as a shop's checkout.

## Back office: what the temple office needs

The public site is only half of the system. The office needs:

- a daily schedule of sevas and pujas with names and details;
- a donation register by fund, date and mode, exportable for the accountant;
- receipt reprinting and correction under controlled permissions;
- reports for festivals: bookings, donations by fund, and annadan sponsorships;
- a simple devotee record (with consent), so repeat devotees do not re-enter details.

For a small temple this can live inside the website's admin. For larger trusts with multiple temples or activities, a separate donor and seva management system connected to the website makes more sense. [Give Setu](/pages/ngopage/), our NGO platform, handles donations, receipts and donor records for trusts and NGOs, and we can extend it with seva booking where needed.

## What it typically costs

Indicative ranges in India for a trust website, not a quotation:

- **Information site** (timings, calendar, visiting information, about, contact, live stream embed), two languages: roughly ₹40,000 to ₹1,20,000.
- **With donations by fund and automated receipts:** roughly ₹1,00,000 to ₹2,50,000.
- **With full seva and puja booking, capacity rules, office schedules and WhatsApp confirmations:** roughly ₹2,00,000 to ₹6,00,000, depending on the number of sevas, languages and integrations.

Payment gateway fees, hosting, WhatsApp messaging charges and maintenance are additional and ongoing. Timelines range from four weeks for an information site to three months or more for a full booking system, mostly driven by how quickly the trust can confirm seva details, prices and policies.

## A simple order of work

1. Agree the list of sevas, pujas and funds, with prices, capacity and receipt treatment, with the trustees and your CA.
2. Confirm 80G and FCRA status in writing, so the donation flow is built correctly.
3. Write the timings, visiting and about pages, in each language.
4. Build booking and donation with the office's daily schedule and reports.
5. Test with the office for a full week before launch, including a festival-day volume test.
6. Launch, announce the official website and UPI details, and warn devotees about fakes.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a temple trust accept donations online?

Yes. A registered trust can accept donations on its website through a payment gateway or UPI, provided the money goes into the trust's own bank account, each donation is receipted in the trust's registered name, and the accounting follows the trust's rules. Foreign donations need FCRA registration or prior permission.

### Do donations to temples get 80G tax benefit?

Only if the trust holds a valid 80G approval, and many trusts with wholly religious objects do not. Some trusts hold approval for charitable activities such as schools or hospitals. The website should mention 80G only for funds that are actually covered, and show the approval number and validity.

### Can a temple accept donations from NRIs or devotees abroad?

Donations that count as foreign contribution require the trust to be registered or to hold prior permission under the FCRA, and must be received into the designated FCRA account at SBI, New Delhi Main Branch. If the trust is not registered, the website should not accept foreign contributions. Whether a particular NRI's gift is foreign contribution depends on citizenship and source of funds, so take legal advice on the wording.

### How do online seva and puja bookings work on a temple website?

The devotee chooses a seva, a date and time within the daily capacity, enters the names and details the priest needs, pays the contribution, and receives a confirmation with a booking reference. The office gets a daily printable schedule of all bookings, and cancellations follow a published policy.

### How can a temple protect devotees from fake donation websites?

Publish the official website, bank accounts and UPI IDs on the trust's own site and social pages, state that the trust does not sell darshan passes through third parties (if true), give a way to report fakes, and keep the site secure with HTTPS, updates, two-factor admin login and backups.
